research_question: Why does chocolate soften and melt in the mouth, and how do cocoa-butter crystals and processing affect its texture?

sources.title: Why does chocolate melt in your hand?
notes: Chocolate's melting range is below typical body temperature, so heat from skin or the mouth transfers energy into it.
Cocoa butter is a major ingredient and its fat composition influences melting behaviour.
Six commonly described cocoa-butter crystal forms have different melting temperatures; tempering favours the form associated with gloss, snap, and a useful melt profile.

sources.title: The science of melting chocolate
notes: Chocolate is a mixture, so it does not have one universal melting point.
Cocoa butter polymorphs have different melting ranges; the stable Form V is commonly desired for eating quality.
Tempering uses controlled heating, cooling, and reheating to encourage a suitable crystal population.

sources.title: The structure and properties of chocolate
notes: Fat crystals can share the same chemical ingredients but arrange into different structures, changing firmness, gloss, snap, and melting behaviour.
Particle size and processing affect mouthfeel; conching helps adjust flavour and moisture as well as texture.
The details of cocoa-butter crystallisation are complex and remain an active technical subject.

sources.title: Molecular Origins of Polymorphism in Cocoa Butter
sources.publisher: Annual Review of Food Science and Technology
notes: Cocoa butter exhibits multiple polymorphic crystal forms with distinct melting points and molecular packing.
The commonly used Form V melts around 33.8 °C in the review's table, while Form VI is listed around 36.3 °C; values depend on the specific material and measurement.
Crystal structure and transformations help explain why tempering and storage influence chocolate quality.

sources.title: The Science Behind Your Easter Egg
notes: Cocoa butter's crystal structure helps determine the chocolate's texture, sheen, snap, and melt.
Tempering is a controlled crystallisation process rather than simply melting and cooling chocolate randomly.
